title: AND and OR from one neuron
objectives: Choose weights and a bias that make one neuron compute AND, and then OR.

screens.title: Both or nothing
screens.prose: Two inputs, each 0 or 1. Make a neuron fire only when **both** are 1. On the plane, the line is where the sum is 0: corners on one side fire and the rest do not. The caption lists the corners that fire.
screens.question: Set $w_1$, $w_2$ and $b$ so the neuron fires on $(1, 1)$ only.

hints.text: Then lower $b$ until only $(1, 1)$ is coloured.

feedback.correct: Your line cuts off the corner $(1, 1)$ alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the caption: only $(1, 1)$ should fire.

explain.text: With weights 2 and 2 and bias −3 the sums are −3, −1, −1 and 1. Only $(1, 1)$ is above 0: the line cuts off that one corner.

screens.title: AND
screens.prose: Fires only when both inputs are 1: that is **AND**. One choice is weights 2 and 2 with bias −3.
screens.question: Fill in the outputs of the neuron (2, 2, −3).

hints.text: Fire only where the sum is above 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A sum of −1 or −3 does not fire.

explain.text: The sums are −3, −1, −1 and 1, so only $(1, 1)$ fires. The neuron computes AND.

screens.title: OR
screens.prose: **OR** fires when at least one input is 1. Keep the weights 2 and 2.
screens.question: Which bias makes the neuron compute OR?

options.why: That is AND: $(0, 1)$ gives −1 and does not fire.
Then $(0, 0)$ gives 1 and fires, so the neuron always says yes.
Then even $(1, 1)$ gives −1: it never fires.

byKey.m3: You built AND. OR must fire when just one input is 1.

explain.text: With bias −1 the sums are −1, 1, 1 and 3. Only $(0, 0)$ stays at or below 0: the line now cuts off the corner $(0, 0)$.

screens.title: NOT
screens.question: What does this neuron output when the input is 1?

feedback.correct: Sum −1, output 0. For input 0 the sum is 1 and it fires: NOT.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the sum, then the threshold.

byKey.sum: −1 is the sum. The output is 0 or 1.

explain.text: Input 1 gives $-2 + 1 = -1$: output 0. Input 0 gives 1: output 1. The neuron flips its input, which is called NOT.

screens.title: NAND
screens.prose: **NAND** is “not both”: it fires unless both inputs are 1. Try weights −2 and −2 with bias 3.
screens.question: Fill in the outputs.

explain.text: The sums are 3, 1, 1 and −1. Every corner fires except $(1, 1)$: not both. Its outputs are the reverse of AND's.

screens.title: At least two of three
screens.prose: Three inputs now, weights 1, 1 and 1, bias −1.5.
screens.question: For how many of the eight input patterns does it fire?

hints.text: Fires with two or three 1s: 3 patterns with two, 1 with three.

feedback.correct: 4: the three patterns with two 1s and the one with three.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count patterns with at least two 1s.

byKey.three-on: 1 counts only (1, 1, 1). Two 1s give $2 - 1.5 = 0.5$, which fires too.

explain.text: The sum is the count of 1s minus 1.5. Two or three 1s give 0.5 or 1.5 and fire. That is 3 + 1 = 4 patterns: “at least two of three”.

screens.title: Must the weights be 1?
screens.prose: A classmate says AND needs weights of 1. “AND treats both inputs equally, and 1 is the natural weight.”
screens.question: Do weights 5 and 5 with bias −7 compute AND?

options.why: Any weights work where only $(1, 1)$ gets a sum above 0. Here it does.
$(0, 1)$ gives $5 - 7 = -2$ and does not fire, so it is not OR.

feedback.correct: Yes: many weight and bias choices give AND.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check all four corners.

byKey.no: You fixed the weights at 1. What matters is which sums are above 0.

explain.text: The sums are −7, −2, −2 and 3, so only $(1, 1)$ fires: AND again. Any choice will do where each single input stays at or below 0. Both together must go above 0.

screens.title: A zero on the corner
screens.prose: Weights 2 and 2 with bias −2 give sums −2, 0, 0 and 2.
screens.question: Which function does this neuron compute with our rule, “fires when greater than 0”?

options.text: AND, only because a sum of 0 does not fire
OR, because two corners sit at 0
options.why: OR would need $(0, 1)$ to fire, but its sum is exactly 0. With “0 or more” it would be OR.

hints.text: Do the corners with sum 0 fire?

feedback.correct: AND: the two zeros do not fire.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply “greater than 0” to each sum.

byKey.or: You let the zeros fire. Under our rule they do not, so this is AND.

explain.text: The corners $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ sit exactly on the line. Our rule says 0 does not fire, so the neuron computes AND. With “0 or more” the same numbers would compute OR.

screens.title: Truth tables in code
screens.question: Write `truth_table(weights, bias)` returning the outputs for (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1), in that order.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each list must equal the expected outputs exactly.

mutants.symptom: A sum of exactly 0 fires, so AND with bias -2 acts like OR.
Lists the inputs in the wrong order, so asymmetric neurons read backwards.

hints.text: Loop over the four input pairs in order.

feedback.correct: Your table lists the four outputs in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: (2, 2, −2) has sums −2, 0, 0, 2: only the last fires. Check `fires` uses `>`.

explain.text:
Run `fires` on each corner in the fixed order and collect the outputs.

```python
for x1, x2 in [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]:
    out.append(fires(weights, [x1, x2], bias))
```

screens.title: One line
screens.prose: Every example so far: $$w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0$$ is a straight line. One neuron fires on one side of it and not on the other.
screens.question: How many straight lines does one neuron with two inputs draw?

hints.text: The boundary is where the sum is 0.

feedback.correct: One line, with yes on one side.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The boundary is one equation.

byKey.two: One neuron has one sum, so one boundary line.

explain.text: The boundary is the line where the weighted sum is 0: 1 line per neuron. AND, OR and NAND each cut off corners with one such line.

screens.title: A risk check
screens.prose: A desk halts trading if its loss limit is hit **or** its price feed is stale. Each is an input, 1 for yes. The check uses weights 2 and 2.
screens.question: Which bias makes the neuron halt in exactly the right cases?

options.why: That is AND: it would halt only when both happen.
Then it halts even when nothing is wrong: $(0, 0)$ gives 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite. It must halt if either input is 1.

byKey.m3: You built AND. A stale feed alone must halt trading too.

explain.text: Halting on either problem is OR: weights 2 and 2 with bias −1. AND would let a desk trade on stale prices while losses were inside the limit.

ideas: AND: weights 2 and 2 with bias −3. OR: the same weights with bias −1. NAND: −2, −2 and 3.
Many weights work; what matters is which sums end up above 0.
One neuron draws one straight line, $w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b = 0$, and fires on one side.

formula.name: The boundary
formula.note: Corners on the positive side fire.

explain.text: Only $(0, 0)$ is below 0. Every corner with a 1 fires: OR.

quiz.prose: The NAND neuron, weights −2 and −2, bias 3.
quiz.question: What does it output for $(1, 1)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the sum, then the threshold.
